terms.definition: a neural network trained to output a copy of its own input, through a narrow middle, so it has to learn what matters in the data.
a model built from many small parts (neurons) arranged in layers; each part does a little arithmetic and passes its result on.
one small part of a neural network: it multiplies each input by a learned weight, adds them up, and passes the sum through a fixed curve.
a group of neurons working side by side; a network is several layers, each feeding the next.
a number the network learns; each input is multiplied by its weight.
generative adversarial network: two networks trained against each other, one making fake data and one trying to catch the fakes.
a model that learns to remove a little noise from an image, step by step; run from pure noise, it makes a new image.
learning from data that has no answer column at all.
a model that can produce NEW data that looks like its training data (here: new images of clothes).
the short list of numbers an encoder squeezes an input into (here 30, or 10, numbers for a 784-pixel image). Also called a latent representation.
the model's own internal summary of an input: its coding. "Latent space" = all possible codings.
the half of an autoencoder that turns an input into a coding.
the half of an autoencoder that turns a coding back into a full input.
the decoder's rebuilt copy of the input; the reconstruction loss scores how far it is from the original.
the one number that says how wrong the outputs are; training changes the weights to make it smaller.
describing each row with fewer numbers (columns) while keeping as much information as possible.
random values drawn from the bell curve, added to data; pure Gaussian noise looks like TV static.
the network in a GAN that looks at an image and outputs the probability that it is real.
the network in a GAN that turns random noise into a fake image.
a convolutional network that shrinks an image and then grows it back, with shortcuts between matching sizes; used inside diffusion models.
a layer that slides a small learned pattern-detector (e.g. 3 × 3 pixels) over an image; CNN = convolutional neural network.
how long one answer takes.
with many numbers (columns) per row; low-dimensional = few.
the narrowest layer, which everything has to pass through.
a function that returns its input unchanged.
principal component analysis: finds the flat surface the data lies closest to and describes each row by its position on it.
turning a value into a short fixed-size code.
a lookup table that gives each ID a short learned list of numbers.
an autoencoder whose coding layer is smaller than its input.
an autoencoder whose coding layer is as large as, or larger than, its input.
the fixed curve applied to a neuron's sum before it is passed on.
no curve at all: the neuron passes its weighted sum on unchanged.
mean squared error: square each difference, then average.
the training method: again and again, nudge every weight a little in the direction that lowers the loss.
for one weight: how much and in which direction the loss changes when that weight changes.
a flat surface (a plane, a line) inside a bigger space.
training where the answers are made from the data itself, e.g. the input used as its own target.
one full pass of training over every training example.
stochastic gradient descent: gradient descent that updates the weights after every small batch.
how big each weight update is.
the algorithm that changes the weights during training, e.g. SGD or Nadam.
the part of Google's TensorFlow library used to build and train neural networks.
Google's library for neural networks; code calls it tf.
an ordinary layer where every input feeds every neuron. (ch02's "dense" was about storing every cell of a table.)
a Keras model that is a straight stack of layers.
in Keras, fix a model's loss and optimizer before training.
a low point of the loss that is not the lowest one; training can get stuck there.
solved directly by a formula, with no training loop.
always giving the same output for the same input.
at right angles to each other.
an autoencoder with several hidden layers on each side of the coding layer.
70,000 small greyscale photos of clothes, 28 × 28 pixels each, in 10 classes (T-shirt, trouser, …).
one dot of an image; in Fashion MNIST each pixel is a brightness from 0 (white) to 1 (black) after scaling.
built in levels, each on top of the one below: strokes, then parts, then whole shapes.
lay the 28 rows of an image end to end as one row of 784 numbers.
the activation max(0, x): negatives become 0, positives pass through.
a method that squeezes many numbers per row down to 2 so the rows can be plotted, keeping similar rows close.
first training a network on a general task (here, reconstruction without labels), then reusing its layers for the real task.
the decoder reuses the encoder's weight matrices, flipped (transposed), instead of learning its own.
a matrix flipped on its side: rows become columns.
a grid of numbers in rows and columns.
the fact that neighbouring pixels belong together.
one layer of an image stack: a greyscale photo has 1 channel; after a convolutional layer there is one channel per filter.
the output of one filter: one number per position saying how strongly its pattern matched there.
in a convolutional layer, a small set of learned weights (e.g. 3 × 3) that detects one pattern.
a layer that shrinks an image by keeping one value (the maximum, or the average) per small block.
a layer that grows an image (e.g. doubles its height and width) while learning how to fill in the new pixels.
making an image bigger, e.g. by repeating each pixel.
how many pixels a filter jumps between positions; stride 2 halves the size.
filler pixels (zeros) added around the edge; "same" keeps the size, "valid" adds none.
the width of a filter, e.g. 3 = 3 × 3 pixels. (Not ch02's similarity kernel.)
removing noise; a denoising autoencoder (b06) is fed damaged inputs and trained to output the clean originals.
setting a random share of values to 0 (during training only).
using a trained model on new data (as opposed to training it).
using a trained encoder's codings as the input columns of another model.
mostly zeros: here, most coding neurons are (almost) off for any one input.
the S-shaped curve that turns any number into a number between 0 and 1.
adding the sum of absolute values to the loss, which pushes many values to exactly 0.
adding the sum of squares to the loss, which shrinks all values a little.
Kullback–Leibler divergence: how far one probability distribution is from another; 0 when they are the same.
an extra term added to the loss to discourage something, e.g. too many active neurons.
in Python, a blueprint for objects: the data an object holds and its functions (methods). (Also, in data: a category, e.g. Trouser.)
a list of possible outcomes, each with its probability, adding up to 1.
a distribution with two outcomes (on/off), like one coin flip.
an autoencoder whose encoder outputs a bell curve (a mean and a spread) for each coding number, and samples the coding from it.
involving chance: the same input can give different outputs.
the bell curve centred on 0 with a standard deviation of 1.
writing a random draw as mean + noise × spread, so gradients can flow through the mean and the spread.
exp(x) = e to the power x; always positive, and the inverse of log.
the Keras way of wiring layers by calling them on each other's outputs, which allows branches.
making the in-between steps from one item to another; semantic = done on the codings, so each step is a real-looking item.
each coding number controlling one trait (e.g. sleeve length) on its own.
a game where one side's gain is exactly the other side's loss.
the usual loss for a yes/no classifier; it punishes confident wrong answers hardest.
Keras: run ONE training step on one batch.
an optimizer that divides each step by a running average of recent gradient sizes.
Adam is a popular optimizer that adapts each weight's step size; Nadam is a small improvement of Adam.
a group of examples processed together in one training step, e.g. 32 images.
a small batch of examples (e.g. 32) processed together.
a state where no player can do better by changing only their own strategy.
a GAN generator making only one kind of image (e.g. only shoes).
one bump of a data distribution: here, one class of clothing.
keeping old fake images in a buffer and training the discriminator on a mix of old and new ones.
giving the discriminator a measure of how similar the images in a batch are, so it can reject batches with no variety.
deep convolutional GAN: a set of architecture rules (2015) that made convolutional GANs train reliably.
rescaling each layer's outputs over the batch to a steady average and spread.
like ReLU, but negative values are multiplied by a small number (e.g. 0.2) instead of set to 0.
an S-shaped curve like sigmoid but from −1 to 1.
a GAN that also receives the class as input, so you choose what it generates.
training a GAN on tiny images first and adding layers to double the resolution step by step.
starting weights scaled by √(2 ÷ number of inputs), so signals keep a steady size through the layers.
dividing each pixel's channel values by their root-mean-square.
the square root of the average of the squares.
a 2018 GAN whose generator injects a "style" at every resolution and adds separate random noise for fine details.
multilayer perceptron: a plain stack of Dense layers.
a neuron's own extra number, added to its weighted sum; it is learned like a weight, and a layer has one per neuron.
multiply by learned weights and add a learned bias, with no activation: a scale-and-shift.
adaptive instance normalization: standardise each feature map, then scale and shift it by numbers taken from the style vector.
denoising diffusion probabilistic model: the 2020 form of the diffusion model this chapter builds.
the fixed recipe that adds a little noise to an image at each of T steps.
the learned opposite: remove a little noise per step, starting from pure noise.
the same in every direction: here, each pixel gets its own noise draw with the same spread.
the list of how much noise (β) is added at each step; chosen by you, not learned.
a wave function between −1 and 1; cos(0) = 1.
the matrix with 1s on its diagonal and 0s elsewhere; here it means "each pixel on its own".
a loss that acts like squared error for small errors and like absolute error for large ones.
a list of sine and cosine values that turns a whole number (here the time step t) into a vector a network can read.
diffusion run on the codings of an autoencoder instead of on pixels, which is much faster.
a well-known latent diffusion model that makes images from a text prompt.
carefully wording the text you give a model to get the output you want.
flagging inputs that look unusual, e.g. ones an autoencoder reconstructs badly.
a research paper posted online (arXiv is the main free site).
the names of big yearly machine-learning conferences where papers are published.
compression that throws some detail away for good (like JPEG photos).
stop training some layers, so their weights stay fixed while the rest of the network trains (in Keras: `trainable = False`).
TensorFlow's name for a block of numbers with any number of axes, e.g. 28 × 28 × 1 for one photo; 32 photos together are a 32 × 28 × 28 × 1 tensor.
a class built on top of another (its parent, or base, class): it inherits everything the parent does and adds or changes only what it writes itself; `super().__init__()` runs the parent's own setup.
one run of the input through the network (or one layer), from start to end, to get its output.
the fixed plan of operations TensorFlow builds from your code before running it.
in statistics, the distribution you assume before seeing any data; here, the standard normal the codings are pulled toward.
the step of training that works out, layer by layer from the output back to the input, how each weight should change to lower the loss.
automatically repeat an array along a size-1 axis so that it matches a bigger array, e.g. one value per pixel stretched across 512 channels.
a single number (a tensor with no axes).
